title: Critical points and polynomial monodromy
subject: specialization
summary: In characteristic zero, simple critical points with distinct critical values force the generic Galois group to be symmetric.
questionsAnswered: When do critical points determine the Galois group of f(x)−T?
Why do simple critical values give transpositions?
Why is the generic group symmetric for xⁿ−x−T?
How can the group change after specialization?

sections.title: Morse polynomials
sections.body:
Let \(K\) have characteristic zero and let \(f\in K[x]\) have degree \(n\ge2\). A critical point is a root \(c\) of \(f'\); its critical value is \(f(c)\). The polynomial is called Morse if it has \(n-1\) distinct critical points and their critical values are pairwise distinct.

Both conditions matter. For \(f=x^4-2x^2\), the critical points \(0,1,-1\) are simple, but \(f(1)=f(-1)=-1\). Moreover, \(f=(x^2)^2-2x^2\) is a composition of two quadratic polynomials. This decomposition gives a block system on the four roots of \(f(x)-T\).

The geometric Galois group is taken over \(\overline K(T)\); the arithmetic Galois group is taken over \(K(T)\). The theorem below determines both.

citations.note: Morse hypotheses and the geometric construction; the quartic boundary example is computed here.

sections.title: The Morse criterion
sections.body:
Theorem

If \(f\in K[x]\) is Morse and \(\operatorname{char}K=0\), then the geometric and arithmetic Galois groups of \(f(x)-T\) are both \(S_n\), where \(n=\deg f\). Its splitting field over \(K(T)\) is regular over \(K\).

Once the geometric group is \(S_n\), the arithmetic assertion follows: it contains the geometric group and is itself a subgroup of \(S_n\). Equality of the groups means that the splitting field introduces no new algebraic constants.

citations.note: The general theorem is applied after base change to the algebraic closure; arithmetic equality and regularity follow.

sections.title: Proof
sections.body:
Work over \(\overline K\). By Gauss’s lemma, a factorization of \(f(x)-T\) over \(\overline K(T)\) would give one in \(\overline K[x,T]\). Its degree in \(T\) is one, so one factor is independent of \(T\). That factor divides the coefficient \(-1\) of \(T\), and is therefore a unit. Thus \(f(x)-T\) is irreducible over \(\overline K(T)\), and its group \(G\) is transitive.

At a simple critical point \(c\), the expansion has the form \(f(c)+a(x-c)^2+\cdots\), with \(a\ne0\). The ramification index at \(c\) is two. Since no other critical point has value \(f(c)\), all other points of this fiber are unramified. An inertia generator therefore exchanges exactly two roots and fixes the rest: it is a transposition.

Let \(H\) be the normal subgroup generated by inertia at the finite branch values. The quotient of the Galois closure by \(H\) is a connected degree-\(d\) cover of \(\mathbb P^1\), unramified except possibly at infinity. If \(r\) points lie above infinity, Riemann–Hurwitz gives

\[2g-2=-2d+(d-r)=-d-r.\]

Since \(g\ge0\) and \(d,r\ge1\), we get \(d=r=1\). Thus \(H=G\): the transpositions generate the whole group.

Make a graph whose vertices are the roots and whose edges are the generating transpositions. Transitivity says that this graph is connected. Edge transpositions of a connected graph generate \(S_n\), so \(G=S_n\).

citations.note: Inertia generation via Riemann–Hurwitz. The graph argument expands the transposition step.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Take \(f(x)=x^n-x\), with \(n\ge2\). Its critical points satisfy \(nc^{n-1}=1\), so they are nonzero and distinct. At such a point,

\[f(c)=-\frac{n-1}{n}c.\]

The critical values are therefore distinct. The Morse criterion gives group \(S_n\) for \(x^n-x-T\) in characteristic zero. Over \(\mathbb Q\), Hilbert irreducibility then gives infinitely many rational \(t\) for which \(x^n-x-t\) also has group \(S_n\).

citations.note: The Morse theorem and specialization framework; the derivative calculation is supplied here.

sections.title: Specializations of a cubic
sections.body:
For \(F=X^3-3X\), the critical points are \(\pm1\), with values \(\mp2\). Thus \(F(X)-T\) has generic group \(S_3\). Its discriminant is

\[\Delta(X^3-3X-T)=27(4-T^2).\]

Examples over \(\mathbb Q\)

  • \(t=0\): \(X(X^2-3)\) is reducible; its splitting-field group is \(C_2\), fixing the rational root.
  • \(t=1\): \(X^3-3X-1\) has no rational root and discriminant \(81\), so its group is \(A_3=C_3\).
  • \(t=2\): \((X-2)(X+1)^2\) has a repeated root. This is a branch value, outside the separable-fiber setting.
  • \(t=3\): \(X^3-3X-3\) is Eisenstein at \(3\), and its discriminant is \(-135\), a nonsquare. Its group is \(S_3\).

citations.note: Cubic discriminant formula and the irreducible cubic group test; specialized identities are checked directly.

sections.title: Positive characteristic
sections.body: In characteristic \(p\), the polynomial \(x^p-x\) has derivative \(-1\). The cover \(x^p-x=T\) is unramified at finite points and has geometric group \(C_p\), acting by \(x\mapsto x+a\) for \(a\in\mathbb F_p\). It is wildly ramified at infinity, so the tame Riemann–Hurwitz calculation in the proof does not apply. Positive-characteristic versions of the Morse criterion require separate hypotheses.

citations.note: Positive-characteristic scope and the Artin–Schreier boundary.

related.why: Specialization relates the generic group to the groups of rational fibers.
Inertia at a simple branch value is generated by a transposition.
A transitive group generated by transpositions is symmetric.
Composition gives intermediate covers and block systems; critical values can coincide as a result.
The family X^n−X−T gives regular symmetric-group extensions of Q(T).
Branch cycles and rigidity extend the connection between ramification and Galois groups.

questions.title: Do separable specializations retain the generic group?
questions.scope: The characteristic-zero Morse family X³−3X−T over Q
questions.body: No. At \(T=0\) the polynomial is reducible, and at \(T=1\) it is irreducible with group \(C_3\). Both fibers are separable. Hilbert irreducibility gives many full-group fibers, with possible exceptional specializations.

citations.note: Specialization framework; the two counterexamples are calculated in this article.
